title: Law Firms: The Shape of Things to Come
author: Nancy Rapoport · Joseph Tiano

dom.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source does not assess the cluster’s contingent claim that faster matters can remain profitable through rates, costs, collections or demand. Instead, it predicts that GenAI will force economic redesign and end hourly billing’s predominance, redirecting attention toward new ways of demonstrating value.
qs: # Law Firms: The Shape of Things to Come  *Nancy Rapoport, Joseph Tiano — Oxford Business Law Blog (2025)*  In our [forthcoming publication](https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=5080449), *we contend that GenAI will forever change how legal services are delivered and will force law firms to re-engineer the legacy law firm economic model.
In a GenAI-powered legal industry, the much-maligned billable hour revenue model will cease to be the predominant way that law firms are compensated.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central economic claim that GenAI threatens the pyramid by shifting routine work away from junior associates, weakening junior-hour revenue and prompting client-driven changes in delivery and pricing. It is more confident than the synthesis about fewer juniors and the decline of hourly billing, but presents these as forecasts rather than measured profession-wide outcomes and does not address the cluster’s training-pipeline concerns.
qs: When routine work moves from humans to computers, the bottom tier of the pyramid will no longer generate the rich results that law firm partners want.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s account of task and workflow reconfiguration, concentrated pressure on routine junior work, client insourcing, and resulting strain on law-firm leverage and pricing. It is narrower and more categorical than the synthesis—predicting the billable hour’s loss of predominance and fewer junior associates—while providing little evidence on verification, user capability, or apprenticeship safeguards.
qs: GenAI can competently handle baseline work; therefore, the firm will need fewer low-level associates.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that GenAI is driving an operating-model and economic transformation that shifts bargaining power toward clients and in-house teams. It specifically predicts client-mandated automation, insourcing of routine work, pressure on junior-leveraged delivery, and reduced predominance of hourly billing, while allowing higher hourly rates for sophisticated work. Its claims are qualitative predictions rather than evidence of a completed market-wide shift.
qs: In a GenAI-powered legal industry, the much-maligned billable hour revenue model will cease to be the predominant way that law firms are compensated.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source strongly supports the proposition that GenAI will disrupt labour-intensive legal production and the leveraged, billable-hour firm model more than it will eliminate lawyers. It predicts automation of routine junior work, buyer-side insourcing and pressure for new pricing and value demonstrations, while reserving lawyers for bespoke and complex work. It is more categorical than the synthesis about GenAI ending hourly billing’s predominance and reducing junior hiring, but does not oppose the cluster’s core position.
qs: When routine work moves from humans to computers, the bottom tier of the pyramid will no longer generate the rich results that law firm partners want.

Some are already shifting their own mix of work, commoditizing parts of it, such as first drafts of routine documents and “first pass” document review and leaving other parts ‘bespoke.’ The beauty of commoditized work, in additional to being predicably income-generating, is that it frees up lawyer time to think about more novel questions and perform more complex work.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s claim that GenAI pressures time-based law-firm economics and requires new ways to demonstrate value. It goes further than the cluster’s cautious synthesis by predicting that hourly billing will cease to predominate, while acknowledging that alternatives have historically gained little traction; it does not address the cluster’s broader buyer-led workflow unbundling, training or verification analysis.

kp.k: GenAI predicted to end hourly billing's predominance
kp.d: Rapoport and Tiano contend that GenAI will force law firms to re-engineer their economic models and demonstrate value through new compensation methods. This is a forward-looking argument linked to their forthcoming paper, rather than a reported empirical finding; they give no deadline for the transition.
qs: In a GenAI-powered legal industry, the much-maligned billable hour revenue model will cease to be the predominant way that law firms are compensated.
Instead, the legal industry will need to develop new ways to demonstrate the value of their services.

kp.k: Hourly economics sustain leveraged pyramids and promotion tournaments
kp.d: The authors connect the staffing pyramid to Galanter and Palay's ‘tournament of lawyers’: numerous junior professionals generate revenue from routine work for a small equity-partner group, then compete for advancement as their work becomes more sophisticated. They identify billable hours as a major advancement criterion and argue that revenue generation is disconnected from actual client value.
qs: The more associates who are billing time at the bottom of the pyramid, the more money the partners at the top of the pyramid can make.

Once junior legal professionals master the scutwork, they get higher-value work, but they also start competing against each other to see which ones will stay at the firm and eventually get to the top of the pyramid.

The ‘road to riches’ in the legal industry is predicated on collecting revenue generated by billable hours whether or not the work handled during a billable hour translated to true value for the client.

kp.k: Profitability and work uncertainty have inhibited billing reform
kp.d: The authors describe hourly billing as inefficient, poorly scalable, problematic for retention and innovation, and ethically concerning around reasonable billing. They argue that alternative metrics have not become particularly popular among non-contingency-fee firms, partly because human work volumes are unpredictable. They attribute persistence to partner wealth and insufficient collective client pressure, not an absence of recognised shortcomings.
qs: None of the other value metrics, such as outcome-based fees, gainsharing, or volume discounts, tried by non-contingency-fee law firms has become particularly popular.
Clients have not had the collective fortitude to effectuate a change.
Despite their recognition of the shortcomings of the billable hour model, law firms have not changed the model because, after all, it is making them wealthy.

kp.k: Automating baseline work undermines junior-dependent firm revenues
kp.d: The authors assert that GenAI can produce useful first drafts and handle baseline work, reducing the need for low-level associates and the revenues historically generated by the pyramid's bottom tier. They describe emerging widespread adoption but provide no adoption figures or performance measurements. They qualify the technology as mimicking rather than thinking and flag graduate job prospects as a concern without developing that topic.
qs: When routine work moves from humans to computers, the bottom tier of the pyramid will no longer generate the rich results that law firm partners want.
GenAI can competently handle baseline work; therefore, the firm will need fewer low-level associates.
they only mimic—but they can often generate useful first-draft material
The shift in billing also makes law school professors nervous about their graduates’ job prospects, but that’s a topic for another day.

kp.k: Powerful clients may mandate automation and insource drafting
kp.d: The authors predict that clients with bargaining power will demand GenAI rather than junior labour for routine tasks. Resource-rich clients may combine in-house lawyers and GenAI to prepare drafts, retaining outside firms for improvements. They argue that either pathway will change delivery workflows and require firms to explain and bill for their incremental value.
qs: We predict that clients with leverage will insist that law firms use GenAI, not junior legal professionals, on routine low-value tasks and that large clients with the right resources will start to pull certain types of work back in-house, perhaps by having a combination of inside lawyers and GenAI develop first drafts, and then handing those drafts to a law firm to ask, ‘how can you improve on this draft?’
Therefore, law firms must figure out how to bill for GenAI-enabled tasks while finding ways to describe their own value-added services.

kp.k: Commoditisation could support a higher-value bespoke practice
kp.d: The authors say some firms are already separating commoditised first drafts and first-pass document review from bespoke work, although they name no examples. They recommend anticipating client behaviour and argue that commoditisation can generate predictable income while freeing lawyers for novel, complex questions. They conditionally suggest higher hourly rates for sophisticated work could stabilise budgets while increasing client value.
qs: The winning law firms in this new type of tournament will be the ones that anticipate this change in client behavior.
Some are already shifting their own mix of work, commoditizing parts of it, such as first drafts of routine documents and “first pass” document review and leaving other parts ‘bespoke.’

If law firms of the future are focused only on high-value, sophisticated work, then they may be able to justify significantly higher hourly rates for that work in a manner that keeps the firm’s budget stable while increasing the net actual value that the law firm is providing to its clients.

kp.k: Demand rebound may enable bifurcated fees
kp.d: Invoking the Jevons effect as a possible mechanism rather than an observed legal-market result, the authors suggest lower-cost production could expand demand for commoditised work. Alongside freed capacity for bespoke services, this could produce flat fees for some tasks and hourly rates of $3,000-$5,000 for work requiring deep experience and creativity. Their prediction retains hourly billing for selected work rather than eliminating it entirely.
qs: Combine an increase in the ability—and the demand!—to perform certain routine work with the amount of time freed up to do more bespoke work, and you can predict that some firms will bifurcate their fees: flat-fees for certain work and billable rates in the $3,000-$5,000 range for work that truly needs deep experience and creativity.
that the fallacy of the billable hour is that all time at a person’s given rate is equally valuable.

kp.k: Future staffing shapes remain uncertain and client-dependent
kp.d: The authors argue that replacing the pyramid's lower layers with GenAI cannot sustain current firm economics. They identify diamond, rocket, cone and starfish structures as alternatives discussed in their paper, without explaining their configurations here. They explicitly leave the predominant future shape unresolved while predicting that client pressure will reshape internal financial models.
qs: That pyramid won’t support current law firm economics, so what other shapes might work?
In our paper, we discuss diamond shapes, rocket shapes, cone shapes, and starfish shapes.
It’s too soon to know what shape might predominate.
Client demand will affect a firm’s shape.
But this time, we think that client pressure is actually going to make a difference in how law firms build their internal financial models.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rapoport and Tiano predict that GenAI will undermine the leveraged staffing pyramid and the predominance of hourly billing, prompting new workflows, pricing and firm structures.
pts.d: The authors contend that GenAI can handle baseline tasks and produce useful first drafts, reducing firms’ need for low-level associates and the hourly revenue those associates generate. They predict that powerful clients will demand AI use for routine tasks, while sufficiently resourced large clients will bring some drafting in-house and retain outside firms to improve drafts. Firms that anticipate this behavior will separate commoditized work from bespoke advice. The authors suggest that sophisticated work could command higher hourly rates, potentially maintaining firm budgets, while lower-cost routine work could experience a demand rebound. They predict that some firms will combine flat fees for routine work with hourly rates of $3,000–$5,000 for work requiring deep experience and creativity. They discuss diamond, rocket, cone and starfish staffing shapes without predicting which will dominate. Their prediction is that hourly billing will lose predominance, not disappear.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers qualitative observations and economic reasoning, with references to other writing, rather than quantified empirical evidence for its predictions.
pts.d: Rapoport and Tiano report emerging widespread GenAI adoption and assert that some firms are already separating commoditized tasks from bespoke work, but give no named examples, adoption statistics, performance benchmarks or measured staffing outcomes. Their mechanism links the existing associate-to-partner leverage model to declining human hours for baseline tasks and increased client pressure. They invoke Galanter and Palay’s tournament account to describe the existing firm structure and the Jevons effect as a possible demand-rebound mechanism. They link their forthcoming paper and an earlier article on billing reasonableness; the supplied blog text does not reproduce empirical findings from those publications. The $3,000–$5,000 hourly range is presented as a prediction, not an observed result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The authors describe adoption and workflow changes as already beginning in 2025, but give no deadline for the predicted economic or staffing transformation.
pts.d: The main changes are prospective and expected eventually as GenAI is used in service delivery and clients exert pressure. Client-mandated AI use is specifically predicted for clients with bargaining power; insourcing is conditional on large clients having suitable resources. Maintaining budgets through higher hourly rates is conditional on firms focusing on sophisticated, high-value work. Increased demand for commoditized work is a possibility rather than a certainty, and fee bifurcation is predicted for some firms rather than all. The authors explicitly leave the predominant future staffing shape unresolved. They also qualify AI capability: the systems mimic rather than think and can often provide useful first-draft material.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect junior lawyers, equity partners, firms, sophisticated practitioners and corporate legal buyers, with graduate employment raised as a concern.
pts.d: Junior professionals, especially first- and second-year associates performing routine tasks, face reduced demand for their work. Equity partners and firms relying on a broad base of associate billings face pressure on revenue and staffing economics. Firms anticipating client behavior are portrayed as likely winners; lawyers doing complex and creative work could gain time and command higher rates. Powerful clients could dictate AI-enabled workflows, and large, well-resourced legal departments could undertake initial drafting internally before seeking outside improvements. The article notes law professors’ anxiety about graduates’ job prospects but does not quantify employment effects or develop a replacement training model. Its focus is law-firm economics and client purchasing, not access to justice.
